title: Question 14691
subject: Criminal Law & Procedure
stem:
Question ID: 14691_vent_helper_lydia
Transformed from: 14691

Peter, a foreign diplomat visiting a Christian law-school banquet, discovered that a small person could enter a privately owned jewelry shop by crawling through an air vent. At a nearby café, Peter befriended Lydia, whom he believed was small enough to crawl through the vent. Without telling Lydia that he was a diplomat, Peter explained the vent route and asked her to help him steal jewelry from the shop. Lydia agreed. Barnabas overheard the conversation and called the police. Shortly thereafter, the police arrested Peter and Lydia. Both were charged with conspiracy to commit burglary. Before trial, Peter moved to dismiss the charge against him on the ground that he was entitled to diplomatic immunity. The court granted his motion. Lydia then moved to dismiss the conspiracy charge against her. The jurisdiction has adopted the Model Penal Code version of conspiracy.

Should the court grant Lydia’s motion?
call: Should the court grant Lydia's motion?

choices.A: No, because Peter's defense does not negate any element of the crime.
choices.B: No, because Lydia was not aware of Peter's diplomatic status.
choices.C: Yes, because a conspiracy requires two guilty participants.
choices.D: Yes, because but for Peter's conduct, no conspiracy would have occurred.

rightExplanation:
A is correct. Lydia agreed with Peter to commit burglary. Peter’s diplomatic immunity is personal to Peter. It does not erase Lydia’s agreement, purpose, or participation.

Gold Key: In an MPC/unilateral-conspiracy jurisdiction, one defendant’s conspiracy liability does not disappear merely because the other party has a personal immunity, incapacity, acquittal, or feigned agreement. Ask whether this defendant purposely agreed to the crime.

Silver Key: When the remaining defendant moves to dismiss after the other person is dismissed, name the axis: other person’s personal defense vs. this defendant’s agreement. Do not chase status knowledge or but-for causation.

wrongExplanations.B: Lydia’s lack of knowledge that Peter was a diplomat does not answer the motion. The issue is not whether she knew why Peter could later avoid conviction. The issue is whether Peter’s personal defense destroys Lydia’s conspiracy liability. It does not.
wrongExplanations.C: This is the dominant trap. It sounds like the common-law bilateral conspiracy idea, but the stem says the jurisdiction adopted the Model Penal Code version of conspiracy. Gold Key: Under the MPC/unilateral approach, Lydia can be liable even if Peter cannot be convicted because of a personal defense.
wrongExplanations.D: But-for causation is the wrong frame. Peter’s conduct may have caused the plan to happen, but the conspiracy question turns on Lydia’s agreement and Peter’s personal immunity. This is not an entrapment problem, and Peter was not a government agent.

c3.label: CUT
c3.text:
* B is not responsive. It answers a side fact: Lydia did not know Peter’s status. That does not answer whether Peter’s defense defeats Lydia’s charge.
* D is not responsive. It answers causation. The call asks whether Lydia’s conspiracy charge must be dismissed.

c3.label: CLASH
c3.text:
A and C fight on one axis:

* A says Peter’s personal defense does not negate the crime.
* C says conspiracy requires two guilty participants.

c3.label: CALL
c3.text: Use the Gold Key because the axis is doctrine-dependent: the jurisdiction adopted the MPC version of conspiracy. MPC/unilateral conspiracy does not require two convictable participants. A remains.
